content: The following professionals were identified as key stakeholders in the context of infant feeding and HIV: pharmacists, laboratory personnel, specialized doctors such as gynecologists and pediatricians, psychosocial counselors, and village health teams. Training for health workers in approximately half of the surveyed countries includes the heat treatment of expressed breast milk. Routine monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems for collecting data on breastfeeding practices are typically integrated into other M&E systems. These systems include those for infant and young child feeding (IYCF), HIV care/prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), nutrition, child health/welfare, and postnatal care. However, the extent of integration varies across countries. For example, 32 countries integrate breastfeeding data into IYCF M&E systems, 14 into HIV care/PMTCT systems, 65 into nutrition systems, 88 into child health/welfare systems, and 76 into postnatal care systems. Some countries also use other systems, while 11 countries either lack such systems or are unsure about their existence. Breastfeeding data is documented in all countries except one, where it is unclear if data collection occurs. This documentation is often included in postnatal care, integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI), or child health registers, including PMTCT/HIV, maternity, and baby-mother follow-up care systems. Four countries also collect this data in community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) registers. Indicators collected include early breastfeeding initiation (9 of 21 countries), exclusive breastfeeding (16 countries), replacement feeding (12 countries), and other indicators such as breastfeeding duration and the introduction of complementary foods (2 countries). However, three countries could not specify which indicators they collect. Longitudinal follow-up of infant feeding practices is rarely analyzed and is documented in only 50% of countries. Most countries disaggregate infant feeding data by HIV status of the child, age group, sex, and feeding practice. However, only one-third of countries receive regular data from at least 80% of their facilities, while another third receive data from less than half of their facilities. The remaining countries are unsure about the proportion of facilities providing data. Challenges in implementing HIV and infant feeding guidelines include shortages of human resources, equipment, and test kits, weak M&E systems, poor adherence to antiretroviral (ARV) therapy, and inadequate patient follow-up. Specific challenges include women returning to work and being unable to continue exclusive breastfeeding, economic barriers to purchasing infant formula, and health care workers' lack of understanding or support for new policies. Some health workers are uncomfortable with recommendations to continue breastfeeding after exclusive breastfeeding due to concerns about HIV transmission risks. Two countries cited a lack of government leadership, and poor coordination between HIV, PMTCT, nutrition, IYCF, and reproductive health programs was also noted. Suggestions for revising the 2010 WHO guidelines on HIV and infant feeding include emphasizing the importance of strong scientific evidence to support recommendations, particularly regarding the safety and benefits of breastfeeding up to and beyond 12 months. Specific proposals include: Removing the phrase in the first six months from the recommendation against home-modified animal milk as a replacement food, as it is not recommended at all. Promoting continued breastfeeding until 24 months, especially when Option B+ is implemented. Differentiating recommendations for HIV-positive and HIV-negative children regarding breastfeeding. Providing operational guidance for treating the entire family in the same facility. Offering guidance on supporting mothers who cannot breastfeed on demand, such as working mothers. Specifying how long women can continue breastfeeding in the absence of ARVs and what to do afterward. Exploring more effective ARV regimens for breastfeeding communities, such as fixed-dose combinations with less frequent dosing. Recommending DNA-PCR testing at birth for HIV-exposed infants. Clarifying when interim feeding strategies, such as expressed breast milk, are appropriate. Addressing financial issues related to infant feeding, including obtaining funds and coping with insufficient resources. Extending breastfeeding duration to 24 months to reduce malnutrition and minimize transmission risks. Reintroducing the AFASS (acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, and safe) framework or a similar concept for decision-making when breastfeeding is not possible. Providing detailed guidance on introducing complementary foods, including what to give, over what period, and how to introduce them. Outlining feeding options for sick or preterm neonates and providing clear guidance for situations where the baby cannot suckle or the mother cannot breastfeed temporarily. Offering more detailed counseling sessions and job aids. Improving IYCF practices at the facility, community, and patient levels. Enhancing M&E aspects of IYCF, including data analysis and utilization. Developing training packages and processes for IYCF. The evaluation of the 2010 guidelines revealed that while implementation has been uneven across 21 priority countries, progress is being made. However, some aspects of the guidance remain unclear, such as issues around complementary feeding and support for working women. Providing more scientific evidence to support new recommendations, particularly for continued breastfeeding after six months, is critical to gaining health staff buy-in. The feedback on confusing content and areas for review will inform the finalization of the 2015 guidelines.
